sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: x]

[MATH: y]

[MATH: k]

The table shows two points on a line in the [MATH: xy]-plane. The [MATH: y]-intercept of the line is [MATH: (k - 1, b),] where [MATH: k] and [MATH: b] are constants. What is the value of [MATH: b?]
sections.readable_text:
| [MATH: x] | [MATH: y] |
| [MATH: k] | [MATH: 5] |
| [MATH: k+3] | [MATH: 17] |

The table shows two points on a line in the [MATH: xy]-plane. The [MATH: y]-intercept of the line is [MATH: (k - 1, b),] where [MATH: k] and [MATH: b] are constants. What is the value of [MATH: b?]

sections.normalized_html:
Since the relationship is linear, it must be of the form
[MATH: y = mx + b] where

  • [MATH: m] is the slope, and

  • [MATH: b] is the [MATH: y]-intercept.

We are given that the points [MATH: (k, 5)] and [MATH: (k+3, 17)] lie on the line and that the line’s [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: (k - 1, b).] So, since the [MATH: y]-intercept lies on the [MATH: y]-axis, its [MATH: x]-coordinate must be [MATH: 0.] This gives
[MATH: k - 1 = 0 \quad\implies\quad k = 1.]

Now, we substitute this value to find the coordinates of the points:

  • [MATH: (k, 5) = (1, 5)]

  • [MATH: (k+3, 17) = (4, 17)]

Then, we use these points to find the slope [MATH: m] of our line: [MATH: m|= (17 − 5)/(4 − 1); = (12)/(3); = 4]

Finally, we find the [MATH: y]-intercept using the point [MATH: (1, 5){:}]
[MATH: 5|= 4(1) + b; 5|= 4 + b; b|= 1]

We use two points to find the slope and set up the equation.

First, we find the slope using the points [MATH: ( -4t, 8)] and [MATH: (t, 18){:}]

[MATH: m|= (18 − 8)/(t − (− 4t)); = (2)/(t)]

Next, we write the line in point-slope form using the point [MATH: (t, 18){:}]

[MATH: y − 18|= m(x − t); y − 18|= (2)/(t)(x − t)]

Then, we multiply by [MATH: t] to clear fractions and bring all terms together:

[MATH: t(y − 18)|= 2(x − t); ty − 18t|= 2x − 2t; ty − 2x|= 18t − 2t; ty − 2x|= 16t]

Therefore, the equation is [MATH: ty - 2x = 16t.]
